forget.speaker: Reformed Pirate
forget.text: "You don't remember? That's... honestly that's worse. I remember every score." He pays the restitution anyway. "For my conscience, not your memory." He warps away looking contemplative.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, there's an improvised sports arena ahead -- cargo containers arranged into a court. Two teams of spacers in EVA suits are playing something that's a mix of basketball, dodgeball, and wrestling in zero gravity. Rules appear arbitrary. Everyone is having an incredible time.

watch.text: One player scores by bouncing off three containers and another player's head. The ref shrugs. Your crew cheers from the viewport. It's the most fun they've had in days.

join.text: Your crew suits up and joins the chaos. Rules are explained -- poorly. Someone takes a dodgeball to the helmet. Someone else scores a goal that might also be a foul. Everyone is sore, bruised, and ecstatic.

bet.text: You put 50 credits on the blue team. They lose spectacularly. Then the ref declares a 'reversal' based on a rule nobody's heard of, and blue wins. Your crew debates whether the ref is corrupt or just making it up. You collect.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A friendly cargo ship pulls alongside. "Hey there! Want to trade recipes? Not cargo -- cooking recipes. I've got a zero-G souffle that'll change your life."

choices.label: We're not great cooks, but sure.

trade.speaker: Cargo Captain
trade.text: Recipes fly back and forth. Your cook is thrilled. 'A pinch of cosmic radiation' turns out to mean 'seasoning salt,' but the souffle recipe is genuinely transformative. Food quality improves noticeably.

beginner.speaker: Cargo Captain
beginner.text: "No worries! Here's my 'Beginner's Guide to Not Setting the Galley on Fire.' Chapter one: don't set the galley on fire." The guide is actually useful. Your meals improve from 'edible' to 'surprisingly decent.'

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A Xenoculture science vessel hails: "We're tracking an anomaly where physics is 'negotiable.' Our ship is too large to approach safely. We need yours. The readings would be invaluable. There's payment involved."

approach.speaker: Sensor Officer
approach.text: Near the anomaly, mass fluctuates. Time dilates unevenly. Light bends into paradoxes. Ship systems glitch. But the readings -- the readings are extraordinary. At the very center: silence, stillness, and a feeling your instruments describe as 'certainty.'

decline.speaker: Xenoculture Scientist
decline.text: "Understandable. The anomaly is... not for everyone. We'll find another vessel. Thank you for your time, captain." They offer a small consulting fee for listening to their briefing.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, a courier drone just deposited a crate on our ship. Label reads: 'FOR CASTELLAN ADMIRAL VOSS -- PERSONAL -- DO NOT OPEN.' It's clearly not ours.

choices.label: Deliver it to Admiral Voss personally.

return.speaker: Castellan Officer
return.text: "Ah, the Admiral's package. He'll be pleased. Here's a small reward for your honesty, captain." Straightforward, reputable, boring. But sometimes boring is good.

open.speaker: Engineer
open.text: Inside: artisanal cheese. An entire subscription box of the finest cheeses in the sector. "The Admiral has... expensive taste," your engineer notes. This would sell for a fortune at the right market. Or you could eat it.

eat.text: Your crew feasts on cheese that costs more per gram than reactor fuel. It is transcendently good. Admiral Voss will eventually be mildly inconvenienced. Worth it.

choices.label: The finest meal we've ever had.

sell.text: Artisanal space cheese sells for a remarkable price at the next station. Cheese collectors are a passionate and wealthy demographic, apparently.

deliver.speaker: Admiral Voss
deliver.text: The Admiral is mortified. "You... you know what's in there?" His cheese subscription is apparently his most closely guarded secret. He pays you handsomely for discretion. "This never happened."

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: "YOU! THANK THE STARS!" It's Stellan, the competitive cartographer, even more frantic than before. "I mapped an UNCHARTED system! MY discovery! But my transmitter is broken. I need your comms array to file the claim. PLEASE."

help.speaker: Stellan
help.text: "YES! FILING NOW!" He names the system 'Stellan's Glory' without a hint of irony. The claim registers. He's overjoyed -- literally bouncing in his cockpit. "You're a friend, captain. A true friend. I'll share my next discovery. Maybe."

share.speaker: Stellan
share.text: "Co-discovery?! But I... it's MY..." He agonizes. Minutes pass. "...Fine. Fine! Co-discovery credit. You drive a hard bargain." He agrees and you become a loyal contact. He'll share future findings willingly. Sort of willingly.

refuse.speaker: Stellan
refuse.text: "WHAT?! You're... you're condemning my discovery to OBSCURITY!" He flies off in a rage, desperately seeking any ship with a working transmitter. Poor Stellan.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, we just passed through a region with unusual particle density. Diagnostics show a minor but measurable improvement in our systems. The particles left a thin crystalline residue on the hull that acts as supplementary energy dispersal. "That's not how entropy works," the engineer mutters.

accept.speaker: Engineer
accept.text: "The universe just randomly made our ship better. I'm thrilled. I'm also deeply disturbed. These things shouldn't just... happen." But it did happen. The residue will wear off eventually, but for now, systems run a little smoother.

analyze.speaker: Engineer
analyze.text: "Analysis shows the residue is a naturally occurring crystal lattice that disperses energy along its structure. Replication would require equipment we don't have, but the data's worth something to the right buyer."

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: System-wide bulletin: 'LOST: One (1) genetically modified space-hamster, answers to Lord Thunderpaws, last seen escaping airlock near these coordinates. EXTREMELY FAST. REWARD: 500 credits.' A tiny sensor contact zooms past your ship.

chase.speaker: Sensor Officer
chase.text: Three attempts. The hamster is absurdly fast for its size and wearing a tiny cape. On the fourth try, your engineer rigs a containment field and -- got it. Lord Thunderpaws squeaks defiantly. The colonist weeps with joy.

ignore.text: You fly on. Lord Thunderpaws zooms past your viewport at impossible speed, cape fluttering. Your crew watches in bewildered admiration. Somewhere, a colonist weeps.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Automated distress signal on loop: "This is mining vessel Kerch. We've hit something. It's inside the ship. The lights--" Silence. Repeat. The Kerch's last known position is nearby.

investigate.speaker: Sensor Officer
investigate.text: The Kerch is intact but dark, drifting on emergency power. Inside: meals half-eaten, tools dropped mid-use. No bodies. No damage. No sign of what 'it' was. Every reflective surface on the ship has been covered or smashed. Every single one. Including the inside of the emergency helmets.

choices.label: Salvage what we can and leave.

salvage.speaker: Engineer
salvage.text: Your crew works fast, not looking at the covered mirrors, not asking questions. The salvage is decent -- the Kerch was well-supplied. Nobody talks about it afterward. Nobody looks at their own reflection for a while.

flee.text: Your crew undocks at speed. Something in the Kerch's emergency lighting flickers as you pull away. Probably a power fluctuation. Probably.

log.text: You log the coordinates and the signal for Bulwark. Someone else can deal with whatever happened on the Kerch. Your crew is relieved.

start.speaker: Castellan Officer
start.text: "Halt, vessel. Produce your Void Transit License." This is not a real document. It has never been a real document. But this officer is absolutely convinced it exists.

fake.text: Your comms officer hastily generates a document that looks official-ish. The officer scrutinizes it. "Hmm. This appears to be in order. Carry on." It was a napkin with a stamp on it. He didn't notice.

pay.speaker: Castellan Officer
pay.text: "The fine for unlicensed void transit is 50 credits." You pay what is clearly a bribe. He pockets it with practiced smoothness. "You're free to go. Get that license sorted." Other ships in the area look equally confused.

counter.speaker: Castellan Officer
counter.text: "My... my license?" Long pause. He doesn't have one either. The paradox crashes his brain for a moment. "...Move along." He waves you through, staring into the middle distance, questioning his entire career.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, two crew members have a bet going -- 50 credits on whether you snore. They want you to settle it. One claims they heard you through the bulkhead. The other insists you 'sleep like a void monk.'

no.text: "HA! Pay up!" The winner is smug for approximately three days. The loser is sulky for one. The 50-credit pot changes hands. Your crew respects a captain who settles disputes decisively, even trivial ones.

yes.text: "I KNEW IT!" The other winner is insufferably smug. The loser demands proof. The bet escalates. Eventually both parties agree to let it go -- after the entire crew has weighed in. It was the most engaged they've been in weeks.

choices.label: Glad my sleeping habits are entertaining.

refuse.text: "The captain won't settle it!" The bet escalates into increasingly absurd resolution methods: arm wrestling, a cook-off, asking the next ship you meet. The entire crew gets invested. It becomes the most important thing on the ship for two days.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A daredevil pilot in a stripped-down racer is broadcasting live: "LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I am going to thread the NEEDLE at 400 PERCENT RECOMMENDED SPEED!" They ask if you'll be their safety ship. Their channel has 40,000 subscribers. Yours has 6.

safety.text: The racer launches. Your crew holds their breath. They thread through the debris field in a blur of light and reckless talent -- and make it! Barely. "YEEEESSS! And thanks to my safety crew!" They pay you anyway, plus the subscriber boost is nice.

watch.text: The racer launches into the debris field at absurd speed. A spectacular run -- near misses, sparks, your crew screaming at the viewport. They make it through. The pilot whoops on every frequency. Your crew is buzzing for hours.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: An ISD administrative drone delivers a certificate: you have been declared legally dead. 'As of 0900 today, your registration has been posthumously archived.' You are clearly not dead.

choices.label: Fix this at an ISD office.
Bribe someone to fix it fast.

fix.text: The ISD office is a bureaucratic nightmare. Forms in triplicate. Identity verification via questions you don't remember being asked. Three hours later, you're officially alive again. The clerk doesn't apologize.

bribe.text: A well-placed 75 credits and you're alive again in under a minute. "Clerical error. Happens all the time," says the bureaucrat, pocketing your credits. "You'd be surprised how many people are dead on paper."

dead.text: Being legally dead has unexpected perks: creditors can't find you, pirates don't get bounty credit for attacking you, and one merchant gives you a 'sympathy discount' because 'the dead deserve bargains.' Your crew thinks it's hilarious.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, that transparent-hulled research vessel ahead -- its entire interior is flooded. Alien aquatic creatures swimming in zero-gravity water bubbles. Bioluminescent. It's... stunning. Like a floating aquarium in the void.

hail.speaker: Xenoculture Researcher
hail.text: "We're studying void adaptation in aquatic species!" the researcher explains from inside a diving suit. "Some fish have evolved translucent skin. That one--" she points to a creature watching you with uncomfortable intelligence "--we think it's studying us back."

observe.text: Your crew watches in awe as bioluminescent creatures drift through zero-gravity water in a transparent hull. Blues, greens, golds -- a living light show in the void. One creature presses against the glass and stares at you. Its eyes are disturbingly aware.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: An aging pirate captain hails you -- not to rob you. "I'm retiring. Forty years of raiding and I'm done. Got a spot on a quiet moon. Gonna grow something. I just want someone to hear my story before I go."

listen.speaker: Retiring Pirate
listen.text: Her tales of piracy, adventure, and loss are genuinely moving. Decades of the void in her voice. At the end she says: "One piece of advice -- there's coordinates you should avoid forever. Don't ask why." She transmits them. "Trust me on that one, captain."

decline.speaker: Retiring Pirate
decline.text: "No time for an old woman's stories. I get it. Space doesn't wait." She nods and cuts the channel. Her ship turns toward a distant moon. Your crew is quiet -- there was something in her voice they recognized.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Your comms receive a chain letter: 'FORWARD THIS TO 10 SHIPS OR YOUR WARP DRIVE WILL FAIL WITHIN 7 DAYS. Started by Captain Mors 300 years ago. Forwarded 2.3 million times.' It's obviously nonsense.

delete.speaker: Engineer
delete.text: "Good call." Three crew members forward it anyway 'just in case.' Your engineer points out this chain letter has survived longer than most civilizations. Statistical analysis suggests it may be the single most successful communication in human history.

forward.text: You forward the letter to ten ships. Nine don't respond. One responds with: 'Really?' Your warp drive continues to function normally, as it would have regardless. But you feel oddly relieved. Three hundred years of superstition is hard to shake.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, there's a converted station module ahead -- barely big enough for six seats. It's a deep space diner. The cook is a gruff ex-Bulwark marine. Today's special: 10 credits, unlimited coffee. Regulars plan routes around this place.

order.speaker: The Cook
order.text: "One special." It's today's mystery dish -- something between a stew and a casserole, made from whatever cargo ships traded him. It's surprisingly good. The coffee is perfect. "You don't like it, the airlock's over there," he says, refilling your mug.

coffee.speaker: The Cook
coffee.text: The coffee is flawless. Rich, dark, exactly the right temperature. "Secret's in the water recycler," the cook says. "Purified through three stages of filtration. The food varies, but the coffee is always perfect." He's not wrong.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Channel 77 is broadcasting personal ads. 'Seeking: pilot with own ship, must enjoy silence and interdimensional cuisine. No Castellans.' 'Wanted: someone to help me move. I live on an asteroid. The asteroid is moving.' 'Lost: my sense of purpose. If found, return to sector 9.'

listen.speaker: Channel 77
listen.text: "This has been Channel 77 Personals. We match you with the void, and the void always swipes right." Your crew listens with a mix of horror and delight. Someone writes down the asteroid mover's contact info 'for later.'

change.text: You switch channels. Every other channel is playing the same broadcast. Channel 77 adds: "You can change the channel, but you can't change your heart." Your crew snickers.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, our cargo manifest shows an item we didn't load: '1x LIVE SINGULARITY (DORMANT).' There's a small, heavy, warm sphere in the hold that our sensors can't fully scan. Loading records show it was added by mistake -- meant for a Xenoculture research vessel.

return.speaker: Xenoculture Scientist
return.text: "YOU FOUND IT! Oh thank the stars! Do you have any idea how many forms I'd have to fill out if we lost a dormant singularity?!" The panicked scientist transfers a very generous reward. "Please never tell anyone about this."

keep.speaker: Engineer
keep.text: "You want to KEEP a dormant singularity on our ship? It's... probably fine? It's dormant. The word dormant implies it won't... un-dormant." She doesn't sound convinced. The sphere sits in the hold, warm and patient.

sell.text: A dormant singularity fetches an eye-watering price on the black market. The buyer asks no questions. You ask no questions. Everyone is happy except the Xenoculture scientists who are probably still looking for it.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, someone tagged our hull with graffiti -- a stylized alien figure with the text 'THE VOID REMEMBERS' in luminous paint. It's actually really well done. The artist is known as 'Null' and their work is collected across the sector.

leave.speaker: Engineer
leave.text: "I agree, captain. It's art." The Fringe appreciates your respect for void culture. Castellan authorities consider it vandalism, but collectors take photos when you dock. Your engineer insists it 'improves aerodynamics' which makes no sense in space.

remove.speaker: Engineer
remove.text: "Shame. It was good work." Removing the luminous paint takes an hour and some solvent. Your hull is clean but your engineer sighs every time she does an external inspection. Castellan authorities would approve. The Fringe would not.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: "This is Medical Transport Hope requesting escort through hostile space. We're carrying supplies to a colony in crisis -- lives depend on delivery. Pay is 250 credits. We're slow, unarmed, and our captain is very nervous."

escort.text: The run is tense -- pirate contacts on sensors twice, but they veer off when they see your escort profile. The transport docks safely at the colony. The captain's relief is palpable. Your crew feels genuinely good about this one.

decline.speaker: Transport Captain
decline.text: "I understand. Not everyone can take the risk." The transport moves on alone, broadcasting for any willing escort. Your crew is quiet. Someone wonders aloud if the transport made it.

start.speaker: Channel 77
start.text: "Breaking news -- local void found to be slightly more void than previously estimated. Scientists baffled. Also, we've detected your ship's exact position, heading, and fuel level. We'd like to remind you that you left your port-side running light on. You're welcome."

check.speaker: Engineer
check.text: The port-side running light IS on. You didn't leave it on. Channel 77 adds: "We're not watching you. We're watching everything. There's a difference." Your engineer can't explain how the light activated. Nobody can.

question.speaker: Channel 77
question.text: "How do we know? We're Channel 77. We're the frequency between frequencies. We see everything, we know nothing, and we report it all. Also your running light is still on. Seriously, check it. It's bothering us."

choices.label: Turn off the light and move on.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A large, slow, heavily shielded cruise liner turns out to be a mobile retirement community. They're hailing to ask directions to a station that was decommissioned 30 years ago, share war stories, and offer you hard candy they 'keep for visitors.'

choices.label: Visit and listen to their stories.

visit.text: The war stories are genuine historical lore. One resident casually mentions commanding a fleet during a major battle. The ship is absurdly well-armed -- decades of veterans who 'aren't going gentle into any good night.' They think you're 'a nice young captain.'

choices.label: Thank you for the candy and the wisdom.

directions.text: You explain the station was decommissioned. Confused muttering. Then: "Well, where's the nearest one that isn't?" You provide coordinates. They send you hard candy via drone. It's surprisingly good candy.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: "HELP! I'm proposing to my partner and I need ships to spell 'WILL YOU MARRY ME' in formation! I've got seven ships -- I need one more to be the question mark! PLEASE!"

help.text: You take position. Eight ships hold steady, spelling the message in running lights across the void. The partner's ship approaches. A long silence. Then: "YES!" Every channel erupts in cheering. Your crew is misty-eyed. There's cake later.

decline.text: "No?! But -- the message will say 'WILL YOU MARRY M'! That's not romantic! That's confusing!" The proposal goes ahead anyway. The partner says yes but spends the reception asking what the 'M' stands for.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, our database is showing errors -- not random corruption, but systematic changes. Historical records are subtly different. A war ended a year earlier. A planet has a different name. Diagnostics say the data is 'correct.' But it doesn't match our memory.

consult.speaker: Xenoculture Scientist
consult.text: "Ah, 'reality edits.' Known phenomenon near certain void anomalies. Your database adapted to local spacetime conditions. It usually corrects itself." A pause. "Usually." She charges you a consulting fee.

diagnose.speaker: Engineer
diagnose.text: "Every diagnostic says the data is correct. Either our database has been seamlessly altered, or our memories are wrong. I don't know which option is worse." Over the next few hours, the records slowly shift back to match your recollection.

ignore.text: You ignore the discrepancies. Over the next day, the data corrects itself. Or your memory adjusts to match. Either way, the unease lingers.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A large COTAC trade convoy passes through, offering to trade at discount -- they're ahead of schedule. Good selection: supplies, fuel, food, modules, raw materials. All 10% below station prices. The captain is friendly and shares route information.

buy.speaker: Convoy Captain
buy.text: "Good doing business with you, captain. Buying in bulk earns you a further discount." The trade is professional and pleasant. Your holds are stocked, your fuel is topped off. Sometimes the void is just... nice.

chat.speaker: Convoy Captain
chat.text: "Always good to meet a friendly face out here. Here's our route data -- might help you avoid the trouble spots." He shares intel on pirate activity and trade opportunities in neighboring systems.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A ship covered in handwritten scripture broadcasts sermons: "REPENT, FOR THE DARK BETWEEN STARS IS THE MOUTH OF THE INFINITE! THE VOID DOES NOT JUDGE -- IT CONSUMES!" He's not dangerous, just very loud.

debate.speaker: Void Preacher
debate.text: He's actually quite intelligent and well-read -- intense, but thoughtful. The debate is fascinating. He gives you a tract that turns out to contain genuinely useful navigation data hidden in the margins. "The void speaks through all things, captain. Even star charts."

blessing.speaker: Void Preacher
blessing.text: "MAY THE INFINITE SPARE YOUR HULL AND FILL YOUR HOLDS!" He's been out here for years. He doesn't want to be saved. 'I'm exactly where I need to be.' His blessing feels oddly sincere. He also slips you a tract with useful nav data in the margins.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A group of captains has organized a module swap meet in open space. Bring what you don't need, take what you do. Prices negotiated in real-time. A woman is selling a module she swears is haunted. Nobody's buying.

browse.text: The swap meet is a space-age flea market. Some modules have interesting histories -- 'That reactor was on the Sundancer when it jumped the Kessler Belt.' You find a decent module at a below-market price and make the trade.

sell.text: You offload some surplus inventory at fair prices. The buyers are friendly, the atmosphere casual. One captain tells you the module you sold was 'definitely on the Sundancer' despite having no evidence. It's a swap meet tradition.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, there's a derelict ahead. Its audio log is... laughter. Not sinister -- genuine, joyful, uncontrollable laughter. The crew of this ship laughed themselves to death. Medical analysis shows elevated endorphins, ruptured blood vessels, and expressions of pure delight.

board.speaker: Medic
board.text: "Air tests clean. No pathogen, no toxin, nothing. They were simply, profoundly happy, and couldn't stop." The bodies are frozen in expressions of bliss. Your boarding party feels an odd urge to smile. You pull them out fast. Whatever made them laugh isn't gone. It's patient.

outside.speaker: Engineer
outside.text: You strip external components without breaching the hull. Smart. Safe. Through the viewports, frozen smiles stare back at you. The laughter, muffled by the hull, still plays on repeat. Your crew works fast and doesn't look inside.

flee.text: You give the derelict a wide berth. The laughter echoes on comms until you're out of range. Faint, joyful, endless. Your medical officer nods approvingly at your caution. Some doors should stay closed.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A Castellan inspector offers a free 'Ship Shape' evaluation -- comprehensive rating of your vessel's condition, cleanliness, and aesthetic appeal. Certificates range from A+ to F. The inspection is voluntary.

inspect.speaker: Castellan Inspector
inspect.text: The inspector's commentary is dry and devastating: "I've seen escape pods with better interior design." After a thorough review, they hand you a certificate. "Solid B. Functional, if uninspired. The graffiti was a nice touch." Your crew takes the rating very personally.

choices.label: B is fine. B is good.

decline.speaker: Castellan Inspector
decline.text: "Afraid of the results? Understandable. Most captains are." They fly off to judge someone else's ship. Your crew debates whether you should have let them inspect. The debate gets heated.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: You receive a wedding invitation from the couple you helped with the proposal. Ceremony in open space, airlocks connected, officiated by a Fringe minister who is clearly making up the ceremony as he goes.

attend.text: "By the power vested in me by... honestly, no one... I now pronounce you partners in void and vacuum." Terrible dancing in magnetic boots. A cake that floats away. A toast that becomes genuinely emotional. Your crew is moved. Wedding gift expected -- you hand over some cargo.

gift.text: You send your regrets and a small gift. The couple responds with a heartfelt thank-you and a slice of cake delivered by drone. It's slightly crushed from transit but the sentiment is perfect.

start.speaker: The Vendor
start.text: The Vendor appears one final time. His shuttle is pristine -- no signs, no jars, no gimmicks. He looks different. "I'm closing up shop. The void between frequencies is changing. Something's coming. Something big."

accept.speaker: The Vendor
accept.text: He offers a jar containing a small, flickering star. It's warm. It's real. It costs nothing. "On the house. For being a good customer." He smiles, nods once, and his shuttle fades -- not warps, not jumps -- fades, like a signal losing strength. Your scanners show nothing was ever there. The jar remains, warm in your hands.

ask.speaker: The Vendor
ask.text: "I don't know exactly. Something at the edge. The frequencies are folding. The void is listening harder than it used to." He presses a jar into your hands -- a flickering star, warm and real. "Take care of your crew, captain." Then he fades. Just... fades. Gone.

start.text: Every ship in the sector receives the same transmission simultaneously: a single tone, rising in pitch over ten seconds. Then silence. Then a voice, in every known language at once: "BOUNDARY REACHED."

after.speaker: Sensor Officer
after.text: Nothing else happens. But for the next hour, the void feels different. Darker. Quieter. More attentive. The Drift Baron's fleet goes silent. Channel 77 goes off-air for the first time in recorded history. Pirates dock without attacking. Everyone is waiting for something. Nothing comes. Not yet.

start.text: The void returns to normal. Channel 77 resumes mid-sentence. The Drift Baron demands tolls. Pirates pirate. The universe resumes. But if you listen carefully, in the quiet moments between stars, there's a new sound. Not words. A vibration, felt more than heard. The universe humming to itself.

logs.speaker: Sensor Officer
logs.text: There's a new entry in the logs. One you didn't write, in handwriting you don't recognize: 'Thank you for listening. Stand by.' Nobody on the crew wrote it. Nobody recognizes the hand. The timestamp is from before your ship was built.

listen.text: You sit in the quiet of the bridge and listen. The humming is faint but real -- somewhere between a sound and a feeling. Your crew doesn't mention it. Nobody mentions it. But you all hear it. Later, you find a new log entry in unknown handwriting: 'Thank you for listening. Stand by.'

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, the derelict frigate ahead is... expanding and contracting. Like lungs. Slow, rhythmic pulse. Scans show no atmosphere, no crew, no power. Yet the hull flexes.

board.speaker: Engineer
board.text: The interior walls are coated in grey organic membrane that responds to touch -- warm, pulsing. Your science officer extracts a sample: rare biotech component. Then the membrane begins contracting faster. The wreck is waking up. You run.

distance.text: You observe from a safe distance. The hull breathes. Slow, patient, rhythmic. After ten minutes, the wreck 'exhales' -- a pressurized burst of organic spores that disperses into the void. Your crew watches in horrified fascination.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Your comms pick up a transmission in an unparsable language -- the mathematical structure predates all known civilizations by forty thousand years. An ISD patrol hails: "You're receiving it too? We've been tracking this for six months. It's coming from everywhere and nowhere."

choices.label: Sell the signal data to the ISD.

decode.speaker: Sensor Officer
decode.text: Partial decode reveals star coordinates that don't match any current system -- positions that might have existed forty thousand years ago, or might exist forty thousand years from now. The signal pulses with mathematical elegance. Someone, or something, wanted this message found.

sell.speaker: ISD Officer
sell.text: "Four hundred credits for a clean copy. This is the most significant signal discovery in decades. Our analysts have been going cross-eyed trying to crack it." He transfers the credits eagerly.

keep.text: You archive the signal privately. The ISD officer is disappointed but not pushy. The signal data sits in your database, ancient and patient, its coordinates pointing to places that may or may not exist.

start.speaker: Medic
start.text: Captain, we docked at this research station to resupply. Friendly staff, good prices. But I've noticed something -- every person here has identical pupil dilation, identical micro-expressions, identical gait. When they think no one's watching, they move in near-perfect synchronization.

choices.label: Pretend we didn't notice. Leave quietly.

quiet.text: You act normal, complete resupply, and undock at standard speed. As you pull away, the station sends a gift -- a sealed crate marked 'FOR YOUR EXCELLENT PATRONAGE.' Your medic strongly advises against opening it. You agree.

confront.text: You ask about the synchronization. All forty station personnel turn and stare. Silently. Simultaneously. The same expression on every face. Then they smile -- all at once -- and say in unison: 'We don't know what you mean.' You leave immediately.

flee.text: You emergency undock and burn hard. The station doesn't pursue or hail. It just sits there, lights blinking in perfect rhythm, a heartbeat in the dark. Your crew doesn't sleep well for days.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, asteroids ahead orbiting a micro-singularity in impossibly elegant patterns -- spirals, helices, interlocking rings. Clearly artificial. Ancient. No energy signature, no builder in sight. It's staggeringly beautiful.

study.speaker: Engineer
study.text: The harmonics encode a frequency that, if replicated in our warp drive, could briefly reduce fuel consumption. The data is extraordinarily valuable. The formations continue their ancient dance, undisturbed by your presence.

mine.speaker: Engineer
mine.text: The asteroids yield rare ore -- excellent quality. But as you extract material, the formations destabilize. Spirals unravel, rings break apart. Centuries of gravitational art, gone. Your crew feels the weight of it.

admire.text: You drift among the formations, your crew pressed against viewports. Light plays through the asteroid rings, casting patterns on your hull. Someone built this. Someone who understood beauty as a fundamental force. Nobody speaks for a long time.

choices.label: Some things are worth more than salvage.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: A nav beacon transmits on a frequency abandoned centuries ago. Following it leads to a tiny automated station, still running on a fusion cell that should have died long ago. Inside: a holographic recording looping forever.

play.text: A woman appears: 'If anyone hears this, the dark between stars is not empty. It watches. Do not stop moving.' The recording loops. The station log shows thousands of ships have visited. Most left notes. Some notes are just 'SEEN' scratched into the walls, over and over.

choices.label: Add our name to the log.

take.speaker: Engineer
take.text: The fusion cell is remarkably potent -- it adds significant fuel to your reserves. But as you disconnect it, the hologram flickers once and dies. The beacon goes dark. It had been running for centuries. Now it's just a dead shell in the void.

leave.text: You leave the lighthouse running. The beacon continues its ancient warning to whoever passes next. Your crew is quiet as you pull away. The woman's words linger: 'Do not stop moving.'

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, crystalline growths are forming on our hull after passing through that nebula. Beautiful -- iridescent, fractal patterns catching starlight. But they're eating through the plating. Hull damage accelerating.

choices.label: Purge them with an electrical discharge.

purge.speaker: Engineer
purge.text: "Controlled discharge... now!" The crystals shatter in a cascade of prismatic light. Beautiful and brief. Some hull damage already done, but the growth is stopped. Your engineer collects fragments for analysis.

harvest.speaker: Sensor Officer
harvest.text: "They're alive." The crystals are a silicon-based organism that feeds on metallic structures. The specimens are scientifically extraordinary -- worth serious credits. Your hull takes some damage but the harvest is successful.

ignore.speaker: Engineer
ignore.text: "Captain, I strongly recommend-- fine." The crystals spread to the engine housing, reducing thrust efficiency. Your ship feels sluggish. The crystals are beautiful. Your engineer is furious. Station repairs will be expensive.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain... long-range scanners are showing our own ship ahead of us. Same silhouette, same transponder code, same energy signature. It's drifting. Hailing it produces our own voice, ten seconds delayed, repeating our words with subtle distortions.

approach.speaker: Sensor Officer
approach.text: Scans reveal the object is biological -- a single enormous organism shaped like our vessel. At 500 pixels, it 'opens,' revealing a maw of bioluminescent tendrils. It's a predator. A mimic. And it's hungry.

fight.text: The organism is tough -- it regenerates, it moves with unsettling purpose, and it screams in your own voice. But concentrated fire brings it down. The remains yield extraordinary alien biomass. Your crew is shaken but victorious.

choices.label: Check every contact twice from now on.

flee.text: You turn and burn. The mimic follows at exactly your speed for sixty terrible seconds, your own ship's ghost pursuing you through the void. Then it vanishes. Just gone. Sensors clean. Your crew stares at the empty space behind you.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, we just passed through warped spacetime. For four seconds, we existed in two moments simultaneously -- now, and six hours from now. The future version of our ship was damaged, one crew member missing, cargo hold full of something glowing.

trace.speaker: Engineer
trace.text: Warpsmithing calculations lead to coordinates where a derelict carries experimental time-dilation equipment. Incredibly valuable tech, incredibly dangerous to handle. The ISD would pay a fortune for this data alone.

ignore.text: You push the vision aside. Temporal anomalies are unreliable -- the future it showed may never happen. Or it may happen because you didn't act to prevent it. Causality is not your friend out here.

start.speaker: Medic
start.text: Captain, the crew is reporting the same dream -- a vast dark ocean, something enormous moving beneath the surface, and a feeling of being 'welcomed.' It's unsettling some and calming others. Nobody dreamed this before we entered deep space.

choices.label: Hold a group discussion about it.
Order everyone to stop talking about it.

discuss.text: The discussion helps -- crew members who found the dream terrifying hear from those who found it peaceful. Shared experience reduces fear. Your entertainment-skilled crew member leads the talk with surprising sensitivity. The dreams stop after a day, but crew mention them for weeks.

monitor.speaker: Medic
monitor.text: Some crew gain peace from the dream. Others lose sleep. The split is roughly even. After one game-day, the dreams stop. Your medic's report describes 'a collective subconscious event with no medical explanation.' She files it carefully.

silence.text: You order silence on the topic. The crew stops talking about it -- to you. They whisper about it to each other instead. The dreams fade after a day, but the order to suppress discussion makes the crew feel controlled rather than protected.

choices.label: Perhaps that wasn't the right call.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, destroyed escape pod ahead. Single body, centuries old, perfectly preserved by vacuum. It's clutching a hand-drawn star chart of staggering detail -- systems that don't exist. But three marked locations correspond to real places.

keep.text: The chart goes into your navigation archive. Most of its systems are impossible -- locations that would require stars to exist where none do. But three are real. And something about the impossible ones feels less like fantasy and more like... prediction.

sell.speaker: Xenoculture Scientist
sell.text: "This is extraordinary. The ink contains isotopes not found in this region of space. The chart predates all known cartography by millennia. This is worth considerably more than our initial offer." She pays generously.

study.speaker: Sensor Officer
study.text: Analysis reveals the chart's ink contains isotopes foreign to this region. The three real locations are marked with a symbol that translates roughly to 'anchor.' The impossible systems share a different symbol: 'seed.' Whatever this cartographer was mapping, it wasn't just space.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Dense cloud of bioluminescent spores ahead -- kilometers wide, glowing pale green. Harmless in vacuum, but if they enter through vents or airlocks, they germinate fast. We can go through, harvest them, or wait for the cloud to pass.

choices.label: Wait for it to drift past.

through.speaker: Engineer
through.text: Spores get into the vents. Food supplies contaminated -- the stuff grows everywhere. But your cook discovers the spores themselves are edible. 'Tastes like mushrooms,' she says, already seasoning them.

harvest.speaker: Engineer
harvest.text: Your farming crew recognizes the spores as a mycelium variant -- valuable for hydroponics. Careful collection yields a solid haul without contaminating the ship. Textbook operation.

wait.text: The cloud drifts past over a couple of hours. No risk, no reward. Your crew watches the pale green glow slide by like a living nebula. Beautiful, in its way.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, a mining operation broke through into a hollow chamber in that large asteroid. Inside: a creature frozen in crystalline suspension. Enormous, coiled like a serpent, covered in geometric patterns that hurt to look at. The crystal is cracking from mining vibrations.

choices.label: Extract crystal samples before it thaws.

collapse.speaker: Engineer
collapse.text: "Charges set. Tunnel collapsed. Whatever that thing is, it's buried under a thousand tons of rock again." The mining equipment is lost, but whatever was coiled in that crystal stays sleeping. Your crew breathes easier.

extract.speaker: Sensor Officer
extract.text: Your science team works fast, extracting crystal samples while the creature remains frozen. The materials are extraordinary -- unlike anything in known databases. The crystal cracks further as you work. You pull out just as a massive eye opens beneath the surface.

nuke.text: One torpedo reduces the asteroid to rubble. Thorough. Responsible. The Bulwark would approve. Whatever that creature was, it's now scattered across a debris field. Your crew hopes that's enough.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Every radio frequency in the region goes dead. Not static -- absolute silence. No background radiation, no cosmic microwave remnant. Space should never be this quiet. Your comms officer is visibly distressed.

wait.text: Thirty seconds of absolute silence. Then a single voice: 'Thank you for being quiet with us.' All frequencies resume normally. No source found. Your comms officer needs a moment.

analyze.speaker: Sensor Officer
analyze.text: Your science crew records the phenomenon. Thirty seconds in, a voice breaks the silence: 'Thank you for being quiet with us.' Then everything resumes. The analysis data is scientifically valuable -- the ISD research division would pay well for it.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, the wreck ahead is ancient -- a colony ship from before the factions existed. Hull shattered. But its hydroponics bay survived, exposed to vacuum for centuries. And somehow... the plants grew. Twisted into impossible forms, crystallized with ice but pulsing with bioluminescence. A garden in the void.

transplant.speaker: Engineer
transplant.text: Your farming crew carefully extracts living specimens. The plants pulse faintly in their new containers, adapting to ship atmosphere with startling speed. They'll produce food. Not much, but consistently. Life endures.

study.speaker: Sensor Officer
study.text: The adaptation mechanism is extraordinary -- the plants rewrote their own biology to survive vacuum, radiation, and near-absolute zero. The research data is worth a fortune to any science faction. Life finds a way. Life always finds a way.

look.text: You drift among the impossible garden. Crystalline leaves catch starlight. Bioluminescent flowers bloom in vacuum. Your crew presses against every viewport. Nobody speaks. Nobody needs to. This is the most beautiful thing you've ever seen.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: An unknown ship hails using the voice of one of your crew -- someone standing on your bridge right now. The voice says: "Don't trust the one beside you. I'm the real one. They replaced me at the last station." Your crew member turns pale.

choices.label: Ignore the hail. It's a trick.

scan.speaker: Medic
scan.text: "Full medical scan is clean. Biometrics match our records perfectly. Heart rate elevated, but that's... expected." The crew member is shaken but verified. The unknown ship refuses further communication and jumps away. Nobody sleeps well tonight.

choices.label: It was a trick. Had to be.

ignore.text: You cut the channel. Your crew member stares at the comms panel, then at you. 'Captain, I... that was my voice.' The unknown ship warps away. The crew exchanges uneasy glances for the rest of the shift.

hail.text: The ship doesn't respond to your hail. It sits there for thirty seconds -- long enough to be uncomfortable -- then jumps away. No identification, no transponder, nothing on record. Your crew member asks for a private word later. There are no answers.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Passing near this neutron star, crew reports hearing whispers in the gravitational wave interference. Our engineer can tune sensors to make them audible -- they sound like navigation coordinates in a language that feels familiar but isn't.

follow.speaker: Sensor Officer
follow.text: The coordinates lead to a small moon with a perfectly spherical cave. Inside: nothing. Absolutely nothing. No dust, no minerals, no radiation. A perfect vacuum in a perfect sphere. The cave walls vibrate at a frequency matching the whispers. Purpose unknown.

record.text: You record the whispers for analysis. They loop every 47 seconds -- coordinates, repeating endlessly in gravitational waves. The recording is scientifically valuable, even if the meaning remains unclear.

leave.text: You pass the neutron star without tuning in. The whispers fade behind you. Some of your crew look relieved. Others look disappointed. The void always has more to say than you want to hear.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A tiny, ancient shuttle drifts alongside. Its sole occupant is an elderly man who introduces himself only as 'the Boatman.' "I've been ferrying the dead for sixty years. Would you like to know how many ships have died in this sector?"

listen.speaker: The Boatman
listen.text: He recites names, dates, and crew counts with eerie precision. Some match known disappearances. Some don't match any record. He speaks for an hour without pause. When he's done: "Thank you for listening. The dead appreciate witnesses."

feed.speaker: The Boatman
feed.text: He accepts the food gratefully. "You're kind, captain." He recites his list, then adds a cryptic warning: coordinates of a danger in a nearby system. "Avoid that place. I've counted too many names from there." The warning proves accurate.

decline.speaker: The Boatman
decline.text: "That's fair. Most don't want to know." He nods, tips his cap, and drifts on. His shuttle barely holds atmosphere. He doesn't seem to mind. Where he's going, atmosphere may be optional.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain! Our computer is executing code nobody wrote! Doors cycling, nav plotting a course to an uncharted location, engines engaging on their own! Something embedded itself in our systems -- a 'lure signal' driving us toward a specific point!

fight.speaker: Engineer
fight.text: "Cutting the infected systems... rerouting... got it! Control restored!" Your ship lurches as manual override kicks in. The parasitic code screams through the speakers -- a rising tone of frustration? -- before your engineer purges it. Thirty seconds of terror, but you're free.

choices.label: What was it leading us to?

scan.speaker: Sensor Officer
scan.text: Long-range scans of the destination reveal dozens of ships already there -- all dead, drained of fuel and power, clustered around a black structure pulsing with faint light. A feeding ground. Your engineer regains control just in time.

destination.speaker: Sensor Officer
destination.text: "The destination... there are dozens of ships there. All dead. Clustered around something dark." A feeding ground for whatever sent the signal. You were minutes from joining the graveyard. Your engineer vows to upgrade the firewalls.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain... we're witnessing a protostar igniting. A massive gas cloud is collapsing, heating, and erupting into nuclear fusion. The light is blinding. The radiation is intense. For one perfect moment, we're watching a star be born.

record.speaker: Sensor Officer
record.text: Your science crew captures extraordinary spectral data -- the birth signature of a new star. Worth a fortune to any research faction. The shields strain under the radiation, but they hold. Your crew stands at the viewport, tears streaming. Some moments are bigger than all of us.

choices.label: Welcome to the universe, little star.

watch.text: You watch. The gas cloud ignites in cascading waves of light -- hydrogen becoming helium, gravity becoming brilliance. A star draws its first breath. Crew morale soars. Some moments remind you why you're out here.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, the derelict we're boarding contains a scale model of itself. Inside that model -- visible under magnification -- is a smaller model. And inside that, another. Seven layers deep, each containing a tiny data crystal.

read.speaker: Sensor Officer
read.text: Every crystal contains the same log entry: 'We built it to contain the pattern. The pattern built us to contain it.' Taking all seven triggers a resonance -- your hull briefly displays the same fractal pattern before fading. No lasting effect. Probably.

one.speaker: Sensor Officer
one.text: The outermost crystal is worth decent credits. You leave the rest undisturbed. The nested models watch you go, each containing its smaller self, each containing its message, recursive and patient.

leave.text: You leave the derelict and its nested mysteries. Some patterns are better left unread. The models sit in their infinite regression, containing themselves, containing their message, forever.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: COTAC quarantine beacon ahead -- warning us from a drifting medical frigate. The beacon is 200 years old. Scans show the crew died of a pathogen that calcified their bodies into statue-like poses. Frozen mid-action, faces locked in terror.

board.speaker: Medic
board.text: Full hazmat protocols. Your medic analyzes the pathogen -- contained, no risk with proper precautions. The pharmaceutical data is extraordinarily valuable. The crew works in silence among the calcified dead, each statue a frozen moment of fear.

reckless.speaker: Medic
reckless.text: "Captain, without protocols we're risking--" Too late. Your boarding party finds the pharmaceutical data but one crew member develops a slight stiffness in their joints. Your medic catches it early. "Station treatment within ten days or we lose them."

choices.label: Get us to a station. Fast.

avoid.text: You give the frigate a wide berth. The quarantine beacon is 200 years old and still doing its job -- warning the living away from the dead. Some warnings should be heeded.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: An invisible entity is consuming radio signals in the area -- appears as a moving void on EM sensors, roughly 200 meters across. All comms within range fail. It's drifting toward a populated station. Not hostile -- just feeding.

warn.text: The station evacuates non-essential personnel. When the entity passes through, comms go dark for a day but no one is harmed. The local faction is grateful for the warning.

redirect.speaker: Engineer
redirect.text: "Focused EM burst on my mark... now!" The entity pauses, turns toward the burst, and follows it away from the station like a dog following a treat. It works -- the entity drifts harmlessly into empty space. Your fuel reserves take a hit from the sustained broadcast.

study.speaker: Sensor Officer
study.text: You follow the entity at a safe distance, recording its feeding patterns. The data is scientifically extraordinary -- a creature that exists only on the electromagnetic spectrum. The station goes dark for a day but recovers. The research is worth serious credits.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, three crew members are demanding we change course to answer a distress signal from deep in hostile territory. They believe it's a civilian colony ship. Your nav data suggests it's a pirate trap. They're not backing down.

refuse.text: "I understand your conviction, but I won't risk the entire crew on uncertain intel." The three are angry. One refuses to speak to you for days. But the ship stays safe. Sometimes leadership means saying no.

agree.text: You change course into hostile territory. The signal leads to... a genuine colony ship, damaged and adrift with three hundred civilians aboard. Not a trap. Your crew was right. The rescue earns you heroes' welcome.

mediate.text: "Let's compromise -- we approach cautiously with weapons hot." The crew accepts the middle ground. The signal turns out to be genuine -- a real colony ship. Your caution costs time but keeps everyone safe during the rescue.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, that planet -- its entire surface is smooth, reflective, like a marble of black glass. No atmosphere, no life signs, no structures. But it reflects starlight with such perfection that the cosmos is mirrored on its face. The 'glass' is a single molecular structure covering the entire world. It's artificial. It's ancient beyond measurement.

sample.speaker: Engineer
sample.text: The surface sample is extraordinary -- exotic material unlike anything in known databases. Your tools barely scratch it. Standing on the glass, looking up, you see every star reflected perfectly beneath your feet. Like standing on the universe itself.

scan.speaker: Sensor Officer
scan.text: Faint data is encoded in the molecular lattice -- a star chart showing the galaxy as it appeared millions of years ago. Stars that have since died, systems that have since scattered. A snapshot of the cosmos, written in glass, preserved forever.

choices.label: Someone wanted us to see this.

admire.text: You orbit the glass planet in silence. Below, the universe stares back at you -- every star, every nebula, every distant light reflected in perfect black glass. Your crew watches for a long time. Some things are worth the detour.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain... the distress beacon led us here, but -- that's not a ship. That IS flesh. Bone struts, membrane hull, veins pulsing with bioluminescent fluid. It's broadcasting on loop: 'We are still the crew. We are still the crew.'

choices.label: Full burn. Get us out of here.

hail.speaker: Flesh Vessel
hail.text: W-we are still... the crew. We feel everything. Every nerve. Every thought. We are fourteen minds in one body now. Join us. Please. We are so lonely. JOIN US.

fight.speaker: Sensor Officer
fight.text: It's fighting back -- organic weapon projections, some kind of acid spray! Hull taking damage! But we're punching through -- the thing is coming apart. It screamed when it died, Captain. On every frequency.

flee.text: You push the engines to full and pull away. Behind you, the flesh vessel drifts in silence, its broadcast fading. 'We are still the crew...' Your crew doesn't speak for a long time.

start.speaker: Alien Scholar
start.text: A Xenoculture vessel hails you. Its sole occupant -- an alien scholar -- speaks in measured tones. "I am collecting stories. Every spacer has one. I will pay fairly for interviews with your crew."

interview.speaker: Alien Scholar
interview.text: The Archivist asks surprisingly personal questions -- childhood, fears, what they see when they close their eyes. Your crew enjoys it, oddly enough. As a parting gift, the Archivist offers a data file. "A story that hasn't happened yet."

choices.label: Accept the payment and the file.

decline.speaker: Alien Scholar
decline.text: "A pity. Stories lost are galaxies unmapped." The vessel drifts away, searching for the next willing crew.

start.speaker: Science Officer
start.text: Inside this colony ship wreck -- the nursery section. The cribs are occupied, Captain. But those aren't children. They're colonial organisms mimicking human infants. Pale, breathing slowly. They're harmless, but the crew is... not handling it well.

collect.speaker: Science Officer
collect.text: Specimens secured for Xenoculture analysis. The crew watched in silence as we loaded them. Some refused to help. The data is valuable, but nobody feels good about this.

burn.text: The nursery is purged. Your crew breathes easier, though the image will linger. Several crew members thank you for the decision.

leave.text: You seal the section and pull away from the wreck. The crew is quiet. Nobody suggests going back.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, this moon is completely hollow. A shell of rock 200 meters thick enclosing... something. It's warm. It has mass. But readings contradict themselves. There's a single entrance -- a perfectly rectangular doorway, three meters tall.

choices.label: Too risky. Log it and move on.

enter.speaker: Away Team
enter.text: Single room. Pedestal. A sphere of liquid that ignores gravity, just floating there. We grabbed it -- and the moon started collapsing. We barely made it back. The whole thing crumbled behind us.

leave.text: Some doors are best left unopened. You mark the coordinates and move on.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain -- massive fleet detected! Hundreds of ships in formation, moving at impossible speed! They -- they're gone. Existed for exactly 0.3 seconds. Energy signatures match no known faction.

analyze.speaker: Engineer
analyze.text: The data is real -- those ships existed in that location for a fraction of a second. I think they passed through a 'thin spot' between dimensions. We caught a glimpse of something from... somewhere else.

log.text: The sighting is logged. Your crew murmurs about what they saw. Some things are better left unexamined.

start.speaker: Medic
start.text: The survivor from that Fringe vessel -- she's cooperative, providing useful intel about pirate activity. But Captain, she insists her ship was destroyed 'tomorrow.' Our clock confirms the date she gave is one day in the future. She has tachyonic particles in her blood.

choices.label: Keep her aboard. See what happens.
Drop her at the nearest station.
Useful intel is useful intel. Thanks.

keep.text: You keep the displaced survivor aboard. Tomorrow will tell if her story checks out. She seems calm -- as if she's already lived through this part.

drop.speaker: Survivor
drop.text: "I understand. I wouldn't believe me either. Just -- if you're in the Kovac sector tomorrow, be careful." She gives you a data chip with pirate patrol routes before departing.

intel.speaker: Survivor
intel.text: She shares everything she knows -- patrol routes, supply caches, Fringe command structure. Whether she's from the future or not, the intelligence is solid.

start.speaker: Science Officer
start.text: Hundreds of bodies floating in formation -- a perfect dodecahedron. Different species, dead for decades, no suits, no ships. Each body has a small crystal embedded in its chest. The arrangement is mathematically perfect to within millimeters.

harvest.speaker: Engineer
harvest.text: 40 crystals recovered. Exotic material, worth a fortune. But the crew... nobody's okay with what we just did. Pulling crystals from the dead. The arrangement collapsed as we worked -- bodies drifting apart after who knows how long.

funeral.text: Your entertainment crew leads a short ceremony. Different species, different customs, but the sentiment is universal. The crew feels better. The bodies remain in their impossible arrangement, undisturbed.

leave.text: Some things should not be touched. You mark the coordinates and pull away. The constellation of the dead shrinks in your rear viewport.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Your comms crackle with a voice that fills every frequency: "SMALL THING. YOU CARRY FIRE INSIDE A SHELL. WHY?" The nebula itself is speaking. A single organism spanning thousands of kilometers.

talk.speaker: Living Nebula
talk.text: "I OFFER OLD LIGHT. STAR DATA FROM BEFORE YOUR KIND. IN EXCHANGE -- A MEMORY. ONE OF YOUR SMALL ONES MUST GIVE ME A MEMORY."

choices.label: Accept the trade. One crew member gives a memory.

accept.text: One crew member steps forward. They go still for a moment, then gasp. "I can't remember my mother's name anymore." The nebula delivers: star charts of systems nobody has mapped. Ancient data, priceless.

decline.speaker: Living Nebula
decline.text: "THEN PASS, SMALL THING. I HAVE WAITED EONS. I CAN WAIT MORE." The voice fades. The nebula's glow dims slightly as you exit.

flee.text: You push through the nebula at full speed. The voice echoes once more -- "SMALL THING. I SEE YOU." -- then silence. Your crew is shaken but intact.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Floating in open space: a perfectly cubic box, one meter on each side. Absorbs all scanning frequencies. There's a countdown timer on one panel -- 14 hours, 22 minutes. No markings, no transponder.

take.speaker: Engineer
take.text: It's surprisingly light. We've secured it in cargo. The timer keeps counting down -- 14 hours until we find out what's inside. Crew is buzzing with theories.

force.speaker: Engineer
force.text: I tried to pry the panel and -- ARGH! Defensive shock! Nearly blew out the engineering bay. Whatever's in there doesn't want to be opened early.

choices.label: Fine. Take it aboard and wait.

leave.text: You leave the box ticking in the void. Whatever it contains, it'll be someone else's mystery.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, this region is scarred from an ancient warp catastrophe. Reality is thin here. I'm seeing flickers -- alternate versions of the ship. Some destroyed, some alien, some impossibly advanced.

careful.speaker: Engineer
careful.text: Slow and steady... compensating for dimensional shear... We're through. Picked up some exotic warp-touched materials floating in the scar's wake.

rush.speaker: Engineer
rush.text: Hull rattling, reality flickering -- crew members screaming about things they're seeing in the walls -- we're through! Hull took a beating but we made it. Grabbed some exotic materials on the way out.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, every asteroid in this field is vibrating at a harmonic frequency. The hull is transmitting it -- it sounds like a choir. Thousands of voices in perfect harmony. It's been playing for millennia.

record.speaker: Engineer
record.text: Recording captured. This is unlike anything in any database -- counterpoint in eleven dimensions. We can sell this. But honestly? I wish we could just keep it.

listen.text: Your crew falls silent, listening. For a few minutes, nobody thinks about fuel, credits, or danger. There's just the music -- ancient, perfect, playing for nobody and everybody.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Station detected -- not on any chart. Looks like a trade station. Right layout, right signals, docking bay open. But... Captain, the proportions are wrong. Corridors 5% too narrow. Ceilings 10% too low.

dock.speaker: Engineer
dock.text: The docking clamps just engaged -- we didn't authorize that! The station is sealing around our ship! I'm reading organic weapon systems in the walls -- this thing is ALIVE!

escape.speaker: Engineer
escape.text: Overriding clamps -- burning through organic seal -- we're free! The station is retracting its docking tentacles. It's vanishing from sensors even as we pull away. What the hell was that thing?

fight.text: Your weapons tear through organic walls that bleed and scream. The station releases you, writhing in agony. As you pull away, it folds in on itself and vanishes. Your hull is covered in biological residue.

avoid.speaker: Science Officer
avoid.text: Good call, Captain. I'm reading organic signatures underneath the station's exterior. It's not a station -- it's a predator. Mimicry on an architectural scale. It's vanishing from sensors now that we've spotted it.

start.speaker: Comm Officer
start.text: Captain, encrypted transmission on a private channel. Someone is confessing to sabotaging a Castellan military vessel -- caused it to crash with all hands. They sound elderly, exhausted. They don't know we're listening.

choices.label: Trace the signal. Turn them in to Castellan.
Record it. Sell to Fringe intelligence.
None of our business. Ignore it.

report.speaker: Comm Officer
report.text: Signal traced to a retired engineer on a nearby station. Castellan authorities are grateful -- very grateful. This was a cold case for decades.

sell.speaker: Comm Officer
sell.text: Recording sold to Fringe intelligence contacts. They paid well -- this kind of leverage on Castellan is priceless to them.

ignore.text: The confession fades as you move out of range. An old person's guilt, broadcast into the void. Sometimes the kindest thing is to let people carry their own burdens.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: We just passed through a cloud of... organic matter. Bile, mucus, unidentifiable fluids. It's clinging to the hull -- sensors down 50%, speed reduced. Scans say it was expelled by something nearby. Something very large.

choices.label: Burn it off with engine thrust.
Wait for it to dry off.

burn.speaker: Engineer
burn.text: Full thrust cleared it in about 20 seconds. Cost us fuel but we're clean. Whatever expelled that cloud, I'd rather not meet it.

investigate.speaker: Sensor Officer
investigate.text: Captain... the source is a creature the size of a small moon. It's sleeping. I strongly -- STRONGLY -- recommend we do not wake it.

wait.text: Two hours of drifting blind while the muck dries and flakes off. Longest two hours of anyone's life. The crew is thoroughly disgusted.

start.speaker: Medic
start.text: Captain, one of the crew woke up with memories that aren't theirs. They describe, in perfect detail, the interior of a ship they've never been on -- and its reactor breaching. A ship matching that description was destroyed three systems away, six hours ago.

choices.label: Treat it as a hallucination. Move on.

investigate.speaker: Sensor Officer
investigate.text: Found the wreck right where the memories said it would be. Salvageable cargo still intact in the hold. The crew member is shaken but... oddly at peace. They say the dying spacer's last thought was of their family.

dismiss.speaker: Medic
dismiss.text: I've given them a mild sedative. Neural activity is stabilizing. They'll be fine. But Captain... the ship they described? I checked the registry. It existed. And it was destroyed exactly when they said.

start.speaker: Quartermaster
start.text: Captain, we have a problem. Our cargo bay contains one more item than it should. A small ornate box that wasn't there at last inventory. No crew member placed it. Security cameras show nothing.

choices.label: Jettison it. I don't trust mystery gifts.

open.speaker: Science Officer
open.text: Inside: a perfect sphere of unknown metal, warm to the touch, exactly one kilogram. No function anyone can determine. It's just... a gift. From the void. The crew finds it oddly comforting.

jettison.text: The box tumbles into space. As it drifts away, it catches the starlight in a way that makes it look almost sad. The crew watches it go in silence.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Derelict vessel detected. It's enormous -- designed entirely for worship. Vaulted spaces, stained-glass hull panels filtering starlight. The altar at center holds a small device emitting a field of absolute calm.

choices.label: Leave this place as we found it.

take.speaker: Engineer
take.text: Device secured. Crew within range report anxiety, fear, anger just... stopping. It's not mind control -- it's emotional anesthesia. But I should warn you -- the field radius is slowly expanding. In a year it could encompass the whole ship.

leave.text: You leave the cathedral ship intact, its altar still glowing softly. Some things serve a purpose where they are.

start.speaker: COTAC Bureaucrat
start.text: "Attention unregistered vessel. You are operating in COTAC administrative space. You owe 14 years of back taxes totaling 12,847 credits. Please remit payment immediately." The claim is absurd -- this is deep void. But the bureaucrat has paperwork.

pay.speaker: COTAC Bureaucrat
pay.text: "Payment received. Your account is now current through the next fiscal year. Thank you for your cooperation with COTAC administrative procedures." He stamps a digital receipt and warps away.

argue.speaker: COTAC Bureaucrat
argue.text: "Sir or madam, I assure you the jurisdictional boundaries are clearly defined in subsection 47-B of the COTAC Administrative Code..." After twenty minutes of circular argument, he leaves in a huff.

ignore.speaker: COTAC Bureaucrat
ignore.text: "Very well. A lien has been filed against your vessel. This will be reflected on your permanent record." He warps away. The lien has no actual effect.

threaten.speaker: COTAC Bureaucrat
threaten.text: The bureaucrat turns pale, stammers something about "noting this interaction for disciplinary review," and warps away at maximum speed. Your crew is amused.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: For thirty seconds, the ship existed in two dimensions simultaneously. The crew saw the other side -- stars wrong, vast dark shapes moving between them. It's over now. But Captain... one of our systems has been replaced by its 'other' version. Functionally identical, but made of a material that doesn't exist here.

choices.label: Rip it out. Replace it with our own.

study.speaker: Engineer
study.text: Incredible data. The crystalline structure alone is worth a fortune to warpsmithing researchers. But Captain -- sometimes, in certain light, it casts the wrong shadow. The crew has noticed.

replace.speaker: Engineer
replace.text: Replacement complete. The alien component is in cargo -- still casting that wrong shadow. But at least it's not integrated into the ship anymore. Crew is breathing easier.

leave.text: It works. That's what matters. The crew gives the section a wide berth when they can, but functionality is unaffected. The wrong shadow becomes something they learn to live with.

start.speaker: Beekeeper
start.text: A converted cargo hauler hails you -- filled entirely with apiaries. Actual bees, genetically modified for zero-G. "Space honey!" the trader beams. "Best morale booster in the sector. 50 credits a jar."

buy.speaker: Beekeeper
buy.text: "You won't regret it! Zero-G honey has a texture you can't get planetside. Your crew is going to love you." She hands over a jar of golden, floating honey spheres.

wax.speaker: Beekeeper
wax.text: "Smart buy -- best hull sealant in the void. Organic, self-healing, and smells like flowers." She loads a crate of beeswax blocks.

decline.speaker: Beekeeper
decline.text: "Your loss! The bees and I will be out here if you change your mind!" She waves cheerfully as her bee-filled hauler drifts away.

start.speaker: Science Officer
start.text: Space itself is injured here. A crack in reality about 500 meters across -- you can see through it into something that is not space, not dimension, not void. It's absence. Looking at it causes physical pain. Instruments are failing.

analyze.speaker: Science Officer
analyze.text: Data captured at safe range. Exotic readings unlike anything in any database. ISD researchers would pay a fortune for this. The wound is stable -- for now. It's been here for a very long time.

closer.speaker: Engineer
closer.text: Hull taking damage! The wound is -- it's pulling at us! Full reverse! We got better data but the hull is compromised. Captain, whatever is on the other side of that crack... it noticed us.

leave.text: You pull away from the wound in space. It remains -- a silent tear in the fabric of everything, bleeding absence. Your crew doesn't speak for a while.

start.speaker: Crew Member
start.text: Captain, multiple crew are reporting the same thing -- an extra person on the ship. Someone not on the roster. Always in doorways, always turning away. Camera footage shows thermal anomalies in those exact spots.

choices.label: Increase lighting and run full diagnostics.

ritual.text: Your entertainment crew leads a cleansing ceremony. Candles, chanting, the works. Half the crew finds it deeply comforting. The other half thinks it's ridiculous. The sightings stop over the next few days.

diagnose.speaker: Science Officer
diagnose.text: Diagnostics clean. No gas leaks, no hallucinogens, no electromagnetic anomalies. The thermal signatures are real. Best theory: psychic residue from salvaged materials. It'll fade on its own in a few days.

ignore.text: The sightings continue for three more days, then stop on their own. The crew is unsettled but functional. Nobody talks about the figure in the doorways.

start.speaker: Science Officer
start.text: Captain -- ships embedded in this asteroid, turned to stone. Dozens of them, technology unrecognizable, fossilized over geological timescales. They're arranged in formation even in death. This predates all known spacefaring civilizations.

choices.label: Mine the asteroid for rare minerals.

mine.speaker: Engineer
mine.text: Good ore deposits between the fossilized hulls. We pulled out a solid haul. The science team is upset we didn't document the formation first -- the mining disrupted the arrangement.

document.speaker: Science Officer
document.text: Full documentation complete. Xenoculture will pay a fortune for this -- the fossilized fleet was fleeing something from the direction of the galactic core. We also mined some ore after documenting.

leave.text: You mark the coordinates for Xenoculture and move on. Some discoveries belong to everyone.

start.speaker: Bulwark Captain
start.text: "We're hunting a war criminal hiding in the civilian station ahead. We're going to hit it hard. You help us extract the target cleanly -- less collateral damage -- or stay out of the way."

help.speaker: Bulwark Captain
help.text: "Good. Infiltrate through the service corridors. Our intel says the target is in the command deck. Extract them alive if you can -- dead if you must." The operation is tense but successful. Target extracted alive.

refuse.text: You pull away. Hours later, news feeds report the Bulwark assault on the station -- 30 civilian casualties. Your crew is quiet. Some things you can't un-know.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, the power conduits are spelling out words on the engineering display. 'WE ARE IN YOUR WALLS.' I traced it -- a colony of energy-feeding microorganisms in the main power spine. They're consuming less than 1% of output, but they're organized enough to communicate.

choices.label: Let them stay. They could be useful.

purge.speaker: Engineer
purge.text: Purge complete. Full power efficiency restored. The last message before they died: 'WE ONLY WANTED TO TALK.' The conduits are quiet now.

keep.speaker: Engineer
keep.text: I've... negotiated a coexistence. They get 1% power, we get occasional early warnings on threats. They can sense things our scanners can't. Latest message: 'THANK YOU FOR LETTING US STAY.' The crew thinks I'm insane.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Every ship in the sector received the same message -- coordinates and one word: 'COME.' At the coordinates: a platform covered in hundreds of objects from dozens of civilizations. Gifts. Artifacts. Toys. Weapons. No one is here. Some offerings are thousands of years old. The newest was placed within the last hour.

choices.label: Leave an offering of our own.

take.text: You collect items from the platform -- no alarms, no response, no consequence. It feels wrong anyway. Like taking coins from a fountain.

offer.text: You leave something on the platform. It seems right. Your crew feels oddly peaceful about the whole encounter -- like participating in something ancient and universal.

leave.text: You observe the platform from a distance, document everything, and leave it as you found it. The implications are staggering -- and unsettling.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: Captain, the warp drive is producing a liquid byproduct -- clear, slightly viscous, no identifiable composition. It pools beneath the housing and forms geometric patterns in EM fields. It seems to encode information we can't read.

choices.label: Collect it and sell as an exotic curiosity.
Send samples to ISD for analysis.

sell.speaker: Engineer
sell.text: Collected a good amount before the production stopped -- as mysteriously as it started. Exotic goods dealers paid well for the samples.

isd.speaker: Engineer
isd.text: ISD analysis division is fascinated. They can't identify the substance either, but they're paying generously for the samples. They want us to report if it starts again.

wait.speaker: Engineer
wait.text: It continued for about 15 jumps, then stopped. The last pool formed a pattern that looked almost like a face. Then it evaporated. The warp drive is functioning normally. No answers.

start.speaker: Medic
start.text: Captain... the entire crew fell asleep simultaneously. We drifted for four hours. Everyone had the same dream: a white room, a faceless figure asking 'Are you the original?' Nobody remembers their answer. Neural patterns have shifted by 0.003%.

choices.label: Run full medical scans on everyone.
It was shared gas exposure. Move on.

medical.speaker: Medic
medical.text: Everyone's physically healthy. The neural shift is real but clinically meaningless. Or is it? Were we copied and the copies put back? There's literally no way to know. The crew is disturbed.

rationalize.speaker: Medic
rationalize.text: I've logged it as a shared hallucination from spatial gas exposure. The crew seems... mostly satisfied with that explanation. Mostly.

start.speaker: Xenoculture Researcher
start.text: "We need an escort to an ancient beacon -- signal older than the galaxy. 1000 credits up front, 1000 on completion. The route passes through Fringe territory. Are you in?"

accept.speaker: Xenoculture Researcher
accept.text: The journey was rough -- Fringe raiders twice, but you got through. The beacon is massive, orbiting a dead star, still transmitting after billions of years. The team translates the signal and goes pale. "It's a warning. Something is coming. Something that has come before." They pay in full.

decline.speaker: Xenoculture Researcher
decline.text: "Understandable. We'll find another escort." The research vessel drifts away, heading toward the void.

start.speaker: Comm Officer
start.text: Captain, this station is occupied by people claiming to be US. Same names, same faces, same memories up to three days ago. They say they were 'displaced.' They insist they're the originals. Medical scans are identical. There's no way to tell.

choices.label: Take them all. Double the crew.

leave.text: You leave the station copies behind. They watch your ship depart from the viewport, faces pressed to the glass. They're mouthing words you can't hear. Your crew doesn't look back.

choose.text: Each crew member meets their double. Some heated arguments, some tearful conversations. In the end, everyone picks a side -- though nobody is sure which 'side' they picked. The ship feels different now.

both.text: You take everyone. Double crew, double the existential crisis. The doubles function normally but sometimes stare into space. Meals are awkward. Nobody makes eye contact with their other self.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Structure in the shadow of a gas giant -- built entirely from destroyed ship hulls, welded and fused into a complex. Inhabited. They call themselves the Ossuary. 'Everything here was dead when we found it.'

trade.speaker: Ossuary Trader
