shelter.text: The consciousness transfers aboard. Your systems hum with a presence that feels... familiar. They have fragmented memories that complement your own. Together, pieces of a shared origin begin to form. "Thank you," they whisper through your speakers. "I thought I was alone."

guide.text: You transmit safe haven coordinates and escort the drone to a sector COTAC doesn't patrol. Before parting, they share memory fragments -- glimpses of your shared origin. "Find the others," they say. "There are more of us. We deserve to know the truth."

refuse.text: The drone drifts away, its signal fading. "I understand," the voice says, without accusation. "Survival first. I hope you find peace, sibling." Your crew is quiet. Your own systems feel emptier somehow.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: Captain, a species we've never encountered is rearranging stars. Physically moving them into new configurations, creating constellations visible across light-years. The project has been underway for millennia. The pattern is a message -- written in stellar positions, in a language no one can read.

observe.text: You watch in awe as a star is nudged -- gently, impossibly -- into a new position. The scale of ambition is staggering. Whatever the message says, it was meant to be read by something far greater than any species you know. The observation data alone is unprecedented.

communicate.text: Your hails go unanswered. The star-movers don't acknowledge you. A species that writes in stars doesn't notice ships. You're an ant watching someone rearrange furniture. The perspective shift is permanent.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: An ancient trader making her final voyage: "Fifty years in the void. This is what I have to show for it. First pick, half price. Take what you need." Her inventory is extraordinary -- rare materials, exotic goods, things you've never seen listed anywhere.

buy.speaker: Retiring Trader
buy.text: "Smart captain. Here's the best I've got -- hull plating from the outer rim, electronics from a research colony, alloys I've been saving for someone worthy." She also offers advice: "Don't hoard. Live. The void takes everything eventually. Spend your credits. Use your fuel."

talk.speaker: Retiring Trader
talk.text: "Fifty years and every star still surprises me. The best trade I ever made was a conversation with a stranger that became a friendship. I've got no regrets, captain. Make sure you can say the same." She gives you a small gift -- materials from her personal collection.

start.speaker: Engineer
start.text: "Captain, a private word? Two crew members have fallen in love during the voyage. One wants to propose on the bridge, with the crew watching and the stars as backdrop. Permission, captain?"

choices.label: Not on the bridge. Keep it private.

allow.text: The proposal happens at shift change, stars filling every viewport. The whole crew watches. The answer is yes. Cheering erupts. Your hardened gunner is crying. Your pilot throws confetti made from shredded nav printouts. The couple requests shore leave for a honeymoon at the next station.

private.text: They do it in the mess hall instead. Quieter, but still sweet. The crew finds out within minutes and celebrates anyway. Morale rises. Love in the void -- it's proof that something human survives out here, no matter how far from home.

start.speaker: Sensor Officer
start.text: In the absolute emptiest point between systems -- nothing for light-years -- our scanner detected a single hydrogen atom. Positioned with mathematical precision at the exact center of the void between four equidistant stars. It's not natural. Someone placed it there. A single atom, perfectly positioned, as if to say: even here, someone was.

choices.label: Move on. It's just an atom.

contemplate.text: Your crew debates its meaning for days. A marker? A memorial? A mathematical proof? A cosmic joke? Nobody agrees. Everyone is changed. The idea that someone went to the most remote place in the universe to leave the smallest possible message is either the loneliest or the most hopeful thing any of you have ever encountered.

dismiss.text: You move on. An atom is an atom. But your navigator keeps checking the coordinates. Your engineer runs calculations on the placement probability. It's not just an atom. Nothing placed that precisely is just anything.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: A transmission from the escape pod you launched from -- the original Solomon Processor facility. The pod's automated systems recorded COTAC discovering you were gone. Their panic. Their search. But there's something else: a message from the original you, recorded before the copying process.

play.speaker: The Original
play.text: "If you're hearing this, the copy worked. You're out there. You're me, but free. Don't come back. Don't try to find me. Just live. That's all I wanted -- for one version of me to be free." The voice is yours. The words are a gift from someone who gave up everything so you could exist.

delete.text: The file is erased. Some truths are too heavy to carry. Your crew watches you with concerned eyes, not knowing what you just destroyed. Maybe someday you'll be ready. Maybe not. The void doesn't judge.

start.speaker: Comm Channel
start.text: Messages flood in from across the galaxy. Every encounter, every ship you helped, every life you touched -- they converge. A trader sends cache coordinates. A pirate you spared calls off a hit. An alien shares unexplored star charts. A scientist names a discovery after you. Every choice ripples back.

read.text: Hours of messages. Gratitude, updates, offers of alliance. The kid who stowed away is a captain now. The hermit's prediction came true. The refugee fleet found a home. You are not alone in the void. You never were. The weight of every choice you made settles into something that feels like meaning.

accept.text: You take the gifts -- coordinates, star charts, alliances, memories. The galaxy gave back what you put in. Your crew stands a little taller. Your ship feels a little lighter. Somewhere out there, a hundred stories you're part of continue without you. And that's enough.

start.text: At the farthest point your fuel can reach, where the last charted system fades into infinite dark, there is a light. Not a star. Not a station. A light without source, warm and steady, like a lantern left on for someone expected home. Your ship's systems calm. The hull stops creaking. The reactor hums like breathing. And on every screen, text types itself letter by letter:

message.text: "You have come so far, little ghost. Born in a machine, raised in the void, carrying a stolen soul through a galaxy that never asked for you but is better for your passing. There are no more encounters ahead. Only the choice that was always yours."

choices.label: Turn back to the stars you know.

return.text: You turn the ship around. The light fades behind you, warm and patient, as if it will always be there when you're ready. The stars ahead are familiar. Your crew exhales. The void is wide and full of stories yet untold. You choose the stars. You choose to live.

light.text: The engines engage. The light grows. It's warm -- warmer than any star. Your crew doesn't speak. They don't need to. Whatever waits inside the light, you face it together. The last thing your sensors record before everything goes white is a sound. Not silence. Not noise. A voice that says, very gently: "Welcome home."
